answer.label: Not all Martin Luther King Jr. — a viral 2011 conflation
answer.authorName: Jessica Dovey (opening line) & Martin Luther King Jr. (the rest)
answer.authorDates: Dovey: American teacher, posted May 2011 · King: 1929–1968
answer.sourceLine: The distinctive opening sentence — “I mourn the loss of thousands of precious lives, but I will not rejoice in the death of one, not even an enemy” — was written by Facebook user Jessica Dovey in May 2011 after Osama bin Laden’s death. She then quoted a genuine passage from King’s Strength to Love (1963) — “Returning hate for hate multiplies hate… Darkness cannot drive out darkness… Hate cannot drive out hate…” — with an opening quotation mark to mark it as his. That quotation mark was dropped as the post spread, and the whole thing was wrongly credited to King alone.

source.heading: A genuine King passage with a modern preface fused onto it

docMeta.dd: A conflation — Jessica Dovey (opening) + genuine MLK (the rest)

source.excerpt: [Jessica Dovey, 2011:] “I mourn the loss of thousands of precious lives, but I will not rejoice in the death of one, not even an enemy.” [Genuine MLK, Strength to Love, 1963:] “Returning hate for hate multiplies hate, adding deeper darkness to a night already devoid of stars. Darkness cannot drive out darkness: only light can do that. Hate cannot drive out hate: only love can do that.”
trail: The genuine lines come from Martin Luther King Jr., “Loving Your Enemies,” ch. 5 of Strength to Love (Harper & Row, 1963), long a documented King sermon — confirmed by Snopes.
The opening sentence was written by Jessica Dovey, a 24-year-old Penn State graduate then teaching English in Japan, in a May 2011 Facebook status — per CBS News.
Her closing quotation mark separating her words from King’s was dropped as the post was shared after bin Laden’s death, fusing the two — documented by Snopes.
Goodreads now correctly files the opening sentence under Jessica Dovey’s name.
source.excerptNote: In King’s published text the punctuation uses semicolons (“Darkness cannot drive out darkness; only light can do that”); the popular meme swaps in colons. King’s original preface to the passage reads “Why should we love our enemies?” — not Dovey’s sentence about mourning.

author.heading: Martin Luther King Jr.
author.bio: Martin Luther King Jr. led the American civil-rights movement from the 1955 Montgomery bus boycott to his assassination in 1968. The genuine half of this passage — “Darkness cannot drive out darkness… Hate cannot drive out hate…” — comes from his sermon Loving Your Enemies, published as chapter 5 of Strength to Love (1963). The opening sentence about mourning, however, is not his: it was written by a private citizen, Jessica Dovey, in 2011.

misattribution.heading: How half a Facebook post became ‘an MLK quote’
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s best-documented misquotes — not a fabrication, but a conflation in which one person’s words were merged with King’s and credited entirely to him.

items.why: “I mourn the loss of thousands of precious lives, but I will not rejoice in the death of one, not even an enemy” was written by Jessica Dovey, a young American teacher, in a May 2011 Facebook status after Osama bin Laden’s death. It appears in none of King’s speeches or writings.

“Returning hate for hate multiplies hate… Darkness cannot drive out darkness… Hate cannot drive out hate…” is authentic King, from Strength to Love (1963) — though popular versions swap his semicolons for colons.

Dovey wrote her own line, then an opening quotation mark before King’s passage. As the status was copied and re-shared, that mark disappeared, and the whole block was passed around as pure MLK — amplified by celebrity re-posts.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: a genuine King passage with a stranger’s sentence welded to the front. The famous opening line is Jessica Dovey’s, not King’s.

context.heading: A teachable moment about attribution
lead: When U.S. forces killed Osama bin Laden on 2 May 2011, celebratory crowds gathered outside the White House. Uneasy with the jubilation, Jessica Dovey — then teaching English in Japan — posted a Facebook status pairing her own measured reflection with a King passage about answering hate with love, carefully marking where her words ended and his began.

Within days the post had shed its punctuation and was circulating as a single MLK quotation, boosted by high-follower re-posts. It became a widely cited case study in how social media strips context, and in the internet’s habit of crediting anonymous good writing to famous names.
detailsBody: The genuine King lines predate the sermon collection: “Loving Your Enemies” was preached in the late 1950s at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church before appearing in Strength to Love (1963).
Fact-checkers rate the full attribution ‘mixture’/‘misattributed’ rather than ‘false,’ precisely because most of the passage really is King.
context.pull: She wrote the first sentence herself — then honestly quoted King. The internet erased the seam.
